strengths: The paper addresses an important phenomenon: strong clean generalization can coexist with robust training accuracy and poor robust test accuracy. Separating clean feature learning from local robust memorization provides an interpretable explanatory hypothesis.
The explicit signal and noise observables U and V make the proposed learning mechanism testable. Connecting representation complexity with training dynamics is a worthwhile objective.

The capacity sweeps and input-flatness experiments provide useful descriptive evidence. For example, the largest CIFAR10 model achieves 86.05% clean test accuracy and 99.57% robust training accuracy, but only 50.08% robust test accuracy.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider a balanced distribution on two points ±e1, radius δ = 1/2, and clean classifier f(x) = x1 − 3/4. This satisfies boundedness, class separation, and the existence of a polynomial-size clean but nonrobust classifier. With a growing training sample, both atoms occur with frequencies approaching 1/2, so vanishing robust training error forces vanishing robust test error; a CGRO classifier cannot exist. Additional distributional and sample-size restrictions are necessary. Furthermore, Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes, whereas Lemma 4.5 incorrectly uses it to assert disjoint perturbation balls for every pair of training points.

The realization argument in Appendix F has another substantive gap: it claims uniform o(1) approximation of the generally discontinuous patched classifier fS by continuous ReLU networks. Softening the indicators does not establish this uniform approximation across their jumps. Nor does small output approximation error alone preserve classification without suitable margin control. Consequently, the stated parameter bound is not established by the supplied proof.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish the robustness required by Definition 3.3. Training attacks are restricted to the meaningful signal direction and leave noise patches unchanged. Small loss against this restricted attack set does not imply small robust training error over the full norm ball. The restricted attack can support a lower bound on full-ball robust test error, but the corresponding training-error implication requires a separate argument.

The dynamics proof contains material mathematical errors. On page 25, a cubic polynomial of Gaussian noise is treated as sub-Gaussian, yielding an unjustified clean-test-error bound; the terms across filters also share the same noise and are generally dependent. Additionally, Lemma 5.11 drops the factor 1−λ from its clean-signal growth bound even though Assumption 5.7 permits λ = 1. At that endpoint, the signal gradient instead scales with the much smaller residual signal α−δ. These issues undermine the claimed phase transitions and generalization guarantee.

The synthetic experiment does not validate the theorem's stated regime: it uses δ = α = 10, whereas Assumption 5.7 requires δ < α. This permits removal of the entire informative patch, confounding poor robust generalization with loss of the signal itself. The real-data experiments illustrate the phenomenon but do not distinguish representation limitations from optimization failures. PGD step counts, step sizes, restarts, repeated-run variability, and sufficient training details are not reported.

The originality of Theorem 4.7 needs clarification. Its existential lower bound concerns a distribution family that already includes linearly separable distributions, and the proof itself constructs linearly separable data. As stated, the claimed extension beyond the cited Li et al. (2022) result appears to follow directly from inclusion of the earlier setting. The useful combined perspective does not by itself establish a stronger lower-bound contribution.

The additional generalization bound in Appendix B also fails as stated. A constant nonzero predictor has zero input-gradient flatness, yet its logistic loss depends on the label. Random fluctuations in sampled class proportions can therefore make population risk exceed empirical risk with probability approaching one half, contradicting the claimed high-probability bound with a zero flatness term. An additional sampling term or stronger assumptions are required.
